entries.title: Animal cell
entries.definition: A eukaryotic cell with a nucleus but no cell wall, chloroplasts or large central vacuole.
notes: Parts (from my diagram): cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, rough & smooth ER, ribosomes, Golgi body, secretory vesicles, mitochondrion, lysosome, peroxisome, centrosome & centrioles, cilium

entries.title: Plant cell
entries.definition: A eukaryotic cell with a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large central vacuole, as well as all the shared organelles.

entries.title: Nucleus
entries.definition: Contains the cell’s DNA and controls the cell’s activities.
notes: Parts (from my diagram): nuclear envelope, nuclear pore, nucleolus, nucleoplasm
Parts (from slide 19): nuclear pore, nuclear envelope, euchromatin, heterochromatin, nucleolus (pars granulosa, pars fibrosa), nucleolar organising centre, rough ER joined to the envelope

entries.title: Mitochondria
entries.definition: Release energy as ATP – the site of aerobic respiration.
notes: Mitochondria = plural, mitochondrion = singular
RELEASES energy – ATP (adenosine triphosphate)
Metabolically active cells have more
The “jiggly wiggly” folds are the cristae
Site of aerobic respiration (Krebs cycle & oxidative phosphorylation)
Can make their own proteins
Can replicate themselves when the cell divides

entries.title: Endoplasmic reticulum (ER)
entries.definition: A network of membranes joined to the nucleus. Rough ER (with ribosomes) makes proteins; smooth ER makes lipids.
notes: Rough ER – covered in ribosomes
Smooth ER – no ribosomes

entries.title: Golgi body
entries.definition: Packages proteins into vesicles and moves them safely out of the cell.
notes: Also called the Golgi complex or Golgi apparatus
Safely gets things out of the cell
Packages & moves proteins out of the cell – covers them in vesicles if they might be seen as dangerous
Close to, but not touching, the nucleus
Transports, modifies and stores lipids (fats)
Assembles glycoproteins
Forms lysosomes
Digestive fluids

entries.title: Ribosomes
entries.definition: Where proteins are made: they read the mRNA and join amino acids together, which tRNA brings in.
notes: Parts (from my diagram): large subunit, small subunit, mRNA, tRNA, amino acid

entries.title: Peroxisomes
entries.definition: Small sacs of enzymes, surrounded by one membrane, that break down harmful hydrogen peroxide and fatty acids.

entries.title: Cytoskeleton
entries.definition: A network of protein fibres that supports the cell, keeps its shape and moves things around inside it.

entries.title: Cell wall
entries.definition: The tough outer layer of a plant cell. It gives structural support and protection.
notes: Tough outer layer
Structural support
Protection

entries.title: Chloroplasts
entries.definition: Plastids containing chlorophyll – where photosynthesis happens.
notes: Plastids containing chlorophyll
Photosynthesis

entries.title: Large central vacuole
entries.definition: A large water-filled sac surrounded by a membrane (the tonoplast). It stores nutrients and maintains turgor pressure.
notes: Large water-filled sac surrounded by a membrane
The membrane is called the tonoplast
Stores nutrients
Maintains turgor pressure – to keep the plant upright

entries.title: Plasmodesmata
entries.definition: Microscopic channels through the cell wall.
notes: Microscopic channels through the cell wall

entries.title: Lysosomes
entries.definition: Release enzymes that digest worn-out organelles and material taken into the cell.
notes: Release enzymes which digest worn-out organelles
Completely break down the cell when it dies
Digest material taken into the cell – take & process dangerous intruders once they die
Exocytosis – exo = exit, cyt = cell

entries.title: Plasma membrane
entries.definition: The cell surface membrane.
notes: Also called the cell surface membrane
Made of: 1. phospholipid bilayer, 2. transmembrane proteins, 3. interior protein, 4. surface markers
Water & other small things can wiggle through the layer into the cell
Small hydrophobic molecules and small uncharged polar molecules get through easily ("ez")
Ions & large uncharged polar molecules need special ways to get in & out, while the others can squeeze through
Cholesterol makes the membrane more or less flexible – lets things in & out easier

entries.title: Phospholipid bilayer
entries.definition: Phospholipids arranged in two layers – the basic structure of the membrane.
notes: Fluid mosaic model: phospholipids arranged in a bilayer, with globular proteins in between
Heads (hydrophilic, "water liker") face the water on the outside and inside; tails (hydrophobic, "water hater") face each other in the middle
Parts (from my diagram): extrinsic and intrinsic proteins, outside, inside, water liker, water hater

entries.title: Integral protein
entries.definition: A protein that goes all the way through both layers of the membrane.
notes: Also called an intrinsic protein (intrinsic = inside)

entries.title: Extrinsic protein
entries.definition: A protein that goes part of the way into the membrane, through 1 layer.
notes: Extrinsic = outside

entries.title: Glycolipid
entries.definition: A component of the cell surface membrane.

entries.title: Glycoprotein
entries.definition: A component of the cell surface membrane.

entries.title: Hydrophilic
entries.definition: Water-loving ("water liker").
notes: philic = likes
Hydrophilic = polar molecule

entries.title: Hydrophobic
entries.definition: Water-hating ("water hater").
notes: phobic = hater
Hydrophobic = non-polar molecule

entries.title: Amphipathic molecule
entries.definition: A molecule that has both hydrophilic & hydrophobic properties.
notes: Contain both hydrophilic & hydrophobic properties
Others are steroids and glycolipids
Phospholipid: head = hydrophilic (polar molecule), tails = hydrophobic (non-polar molecule)

entries.title: Micelle
entries.definition: A structure formed by amphipathic molecules.
notes: A ball of phospholipids in water: heads face the water, tails hide in the middle (from my diagram)
